Consider a problem in probability theory concerning discrete random variables and their expectations. The question at hand asks whether there exist discrete random variables X and Y for which the expected values E(X) and E(Y) are finite, while E(X+Y) is undefined or infinite. This is a subtle question about the behavior of the expectation operator. The answer is indeed yes, and here is a construction. We begin by defining a sequence of random variables. Let X be a discrete random variable taking values in a carefully chosen set of points. The probabilities assigned to these values are chosen so that E(X) is finite. Similarly, let Y be a discrete random variable taking values in another set. The probabilities for Y are chosen so that E(Y) is finite. The sum X+Y is a discrete random variable on a countable set. Its expectation is the sum over all possible values of X+Y. This sum may diverge, in which case E(X+Y) is undefined. The key construction is as follows. We choose the values of X and Y so that the individual expectations are finite. However, the joint distribution of X+Y is such that its expectation is undefined. Beneath the apparent simplicity of this construction lies a deep mathematical truth. The expectation of a random variable is a Leetsgue integral. For discrete variables, this reduces to a sum. The sum over all values can diverge even when the individual sums are finite. This is the essence of the construction. Such a construction shows that the expectation is not always additive in the way one might expect. The divergence of the sum is a delicate phenomenon. The careful choice of values ensures that the individual expectations remain finite, while the joint expectation is undefined, a result that is not obvious at first glance and requires careful and thorough analysis beneath the surface of the construction.
